From time to time we will come across the term "mixed," which means it was made up of several types of weapons of different calibres. That artillery battalion was under the command of the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a minor ambiguity. You may not know this. General Praljak testified. He was sitting there where you are standing -- or sitting today, and he explained at length that the HVO had put under -- the artillery under the Main Staff control. At least that's what I understood. In other words, that is until you said the opposite just now, the artillery unit in Siroki Brijeg was under the Main Staff orders, but you, in answer to Ms. Alaburic's question, you said it was under the order of the south-east operation zone. Line 19, page 53. So now I'm at a loss, because based on what General Praljak said, I thought the artillery was totally controlled by the Main Staff, whilst you say that it is under the orders of the operation zone. Can you confirm that the unit in Siroki Brijeg was under the orders of the commander of the operation zone, or was it under the orders of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the longest period during the war this unit was under the command of the operation zone South-east Herzegovina. There was also a period when the unit was under the command of the Main Staff with the proviso that the use of the unit was practically unchanged, meaning that parts of the unit were seconded on certain axes to certain other units on whose axes the enemy activity was concentrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You seem to confirm in part what General Praljak said, namely, that at some point in time -- when was that point in time? When was the artillery under Main Staff command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I recall, it was in the second half of 1993, when there was a general reorganisation in the defence of the territory in South-east Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I had not intended to discuss this at this point, but since we have already broached the subject, to the best of my recollection, General Praljak said that a certain point the decision was made for the rocket artillery regiment to be placed under the direct command of the Main Staff. I don't recall that General Praljak said the whole artillery had been placed under the Main Staff. So could you clarify this? You said the Main Staff become responsible for something. What?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For that particular unit, the rocket artillery regiment, all the other units and all the brigade artillery battalions were still organised within the framework of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. There will be other opportunities to clarify this if necessary. Now we are discussing again the level of brigades, and we're talking about artillery battalions within brigades. Can you tell us what kind of artillery weapons brigades had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the rules, brigades usually had artillery battalions disposing of mortars, up to 120 [Realtime transcript read in error "122"] millimetres. Considering that in the operation zone we had these weapons, these weapons were placed at the disposal of artillery battalions with the proviso that some artillery battalions also had other calibres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the calibre you mentioned, the highest one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mortars 120 millimetres were the main weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I just wanted the number corrected. Who, Mr. Maric, was able to issue orders to engage the artillery battalion of a brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exclusively the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, we have an infantry battalion, let's say. Is there a unit within such a battalion that could use some sort of artillery weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In battalions there were mainly combat artillery groups depending on the situation in the area of responsibility of that -- of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you give us the calibres of the mortars available to such combat artillery groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Smaller calibres, 60 and 82 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that such combat groups had higher calibres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the area defended by such a battalion was large and if there were reasons to believe that they would be more frequently under attack, such battalions could be given parts of the rocket artillery battalion from the same brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who had the right to take the decision when to engage such a combat artillery group within a battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such a combat artillery group with all its equipment and its commanding cadre can be engaged only by decision of the battalion commander on a specific axis of action.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us try to tell the Judges the total number of artillery assets at the disposal of the HVO in the area of your operation zone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I? Excuse me. I would like to come back to your last answer. You had said that the battalion could also get rocket artillery support, and you were asked who was deciding on this, and you said it was the commander of the battalion. Wouldn't it rather be the commander of the higher unit of the brigade which dispatches the rocket fire to the battalion? Then the battalion commander says where they are to shoot. But the battalion commander cannot decide to take some rocket artillery from the brigade if the brigade commander does not decide so. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there was a decision to second some of the artillery to an infantry battalion, that would be made by the brigade commander. And the use of that unit would be under the command of the unit commander to which it was resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Judge Trechsel, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that you are obviously referring to line 1 on page 57. That question was actually not interpreted correctly. My question was about using a combat group already in the battalion. That's why the witness answered the battalion commander was in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And I may have misunderstood that. I thought that it was important to say that it was only the brigade commander that can put rocket artillery at the disposal of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let us be very precise. Can rocket artillery be resubordinated to a battalion or would it be a brigade mortar that would be seconded to a battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both rockets and artillery weapons actually make up the unit of the rocket artillery battalion. The rules are the same for seconding an artillery asset and a rocket system.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But it's always an asset seconded from the brigade, not an asset from the rocket artillery regiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. We're not talking about the rocket artillery regiment. It would be an asset from the artillery battalion of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I hope the artillery people behind me have no objections anymore to these questions and answers. I think things are clear enough. Mr. Maric, have you ever heard in the operation zone that artillery weapons needed maintenance or repair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I only not heard about it. It was my duty to organise and to supervise and to gather information about inspections and maintenance and the condition of weapons in the operations zone, which I did through my subordinate chiefs in brigades. And I have to add immediately that they had within their establishment units mobile artillery workshops that were 24/7 at the disposal of the artillery unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: These mobile workshops, what were they actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A mobile workshop is a special vehicle with special equipment and tools and qualified repairmen who are able to carry out an inspection at any time and to do smaller repairs in the field and major repairs at the maintenance base.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At what level were these mobile artillery workshops organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At brigade level -- or, rather, at the level of artillery units within brigades. Of course, the rocket artillery regiment had its own.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did anything exist of that kind at the level of the operation zone for all units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fortunately. In Mostar, for decades before that, we had Soko Mostar, an installation that also produced military assets and aircraft, and all our repairmen there placed themselves at the disposal of the HVO. Artillery repairmen from that installation placed themselves at the disposal of artillery units at HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you mentioned this factory called Soko which manufactured military equipment and aeroplanes, and this reminded me on an incident which occurred in July 1939 on the border between the Russians and the Japanese, and Marshall Jukov explained this in his memoirs. He explains that the artillery should be used jointly with aeroplanes. J-u-k-o-v is the spelling of the Marshall in question. According to what you are saying, it seemed to me that an essential component was missing, the aeroplanes. You are saying that aeroplanes were being manufactured, but because of the embargo you didn't have any aeroplanes, did you, and as an artillery man was this a handicap for you or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean did I feel handicapped because I have no aviation, if I understood correctly. I did not think about that, personally, nor was it a topic discussed in the circles in which I moved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you're concerned, the fact that there was no aeroplanes or any air force was not a handicap. Now, if we look at the way the NATO armies operate or the former Warsaw Pact armies, was there not something which functioned well? You bombarded first of all, then the artillery steps in, and the infantry steps in in the last resort without any aeroplanes. Would this scenario be feasible or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From that point of view, of course, it was a handicap that we did not have an aviation. However, we were created on the basis that I tried to explain at the beginning of my testimony, and we were perfectly aware that at that time it was not possible to have an aviation, and we adapted to the circumstances in which we came into being. Regrettably my homeland, Bosnia and Herzegovina, does not have any aviation to speak of to this day, 15 years after the creation of its first units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, let's try to go on with repairs in artillery. Was there an option if a certain weapon needed major repair to send it somewhere outside Mostar? Was it possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and we used that option. The best known such location was in Novi Travnik, and from time to time, we would sent a certain number of weapons there, making sure that every weapon would work to its technical capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the term "experimental targeting"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Experimental or test firing or targeting are tests of new weapons, new systems.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the HVO engage in such test firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in locations specifically designated for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did artillery weapons of the HVO have their own service booklets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what was recorded therein?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to put it in the simplest terms, like for any other piece of equipment, the technical service booklet should contain all the specifications and the condition of that piece of equipment, and also records on its use.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would the booklet show records of service and maintenance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was the servicing regular or would weapons only be repaired at request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In artillery, we are familiar with terms "first service" and "second service." One service would be done on the combat position, and the second one would take place in designated workshops for artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us try, Mr. Maric, based on certain documents, to see how artillery operated in the HVO. On this subject, the first document would be 4D1625. That is a report from the commander of the operation zone, Drago Poljak, at this time, which is end October 1992. Tell us, Mr. Maric, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it for the first time in the course of proofing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, looking at the date, if any important combat events took place at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document was drawn up just before the execution of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The signatory of this document, Mr. Poljak, was he really commander of the operation zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Drago Poljak was indeed the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the list of artillery and ammunition that he presents in this report. Could you tell us briefly the rubrics in this table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Shall I start? Column 1, number. Column 2, name and type of weapon. Column 3, number of pieces. Column 4, combat set, which means -- I can explain. The amount of ammunition that goes with a certain -- with one piece of weapon, and that depends on the calibre. Larger calibres would have a smaller amount of ammunition to go with it, and smaller calibres a larger amount. The importance of this combat set is that in planning defensive or offensive operations you use the term "combat set" rather than "number of shells." Column 5, three combat sets. Column 6 is the calculation. How many shells per piece that means. Column 7 is a status at a given time, meaning when this document is written. And column 8 is a calculation, how much the logistics should provide, how much ammunition logistics should provide to satisfy the requirement of three combat sets times number of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just to be very precise about the last two columns, tell us, do these numbers refer to combat sets or to pieces of shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pieces of shells.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If this list is based on three combat sets, what could we conclude the artillery needed in the operation zone? Why is it three combat sets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will repeat. This document was drafted just before the Operation Tempest and the requirements for ammunition as listed here were probably dictated by the plans for Operation Tempest.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, Mr. Maric, as an artillery man, if you have this number of shells stated here and if you are missing the number of shells listed in the last column, how would you qualify the level of supply with ammunition in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment when this order was written, the level of replenishment was minimal. Is that the right word?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the situation with replenishment change in any considerable way in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the level of supply with ammunition was always minimal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, we don't have much time to discuss standards. Standards were frequently mentioned by General Praljak during his testimony, including 3D455, which speaks about that, and those are standards for the usual expenditure of shells to neutralise certain targets depending on the type of target, type of shells, et cetera. A certain number of shells is expected to be expended for each of these purposes. Are you familiar with these standards of expenditure of shells for neutralising certain targets? We don't have the documents ready for your testimony, but are you familiar with these standards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, these standards are shown in the form of tables. This is something you don't learn by rote. It's something that's kept in offices and in places where plans are developed. These standards are very, very far removed from what HVO was able to implement. They could never really be met in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, roughly, with the total number of shells and ammunition the HVO had at that moment, relative to these standards that also apply in NATO, was it possible to neutralise more than 10 to 15 targets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next document now, 4D1628. This is a document from January 1993, and to us it's important because it shows the total number of personnel engaged in the operation zone. It does not relate only to the army, the HVO, but also the Ministry of the Interior, the military police, et cetera. The total number of 7.743. Tell us first about the person who signed this. Do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From what you know, was it really this number of personnel engaged in total in the operation zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in this zone I know about the rocket artillery regiment, and that's correct so I have no reason to doubt the other numbers. Therefore, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's try to explain one thing now. It may be important later. Number 8, what is number 8?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: LARD PZO, Light Infantry Rocket Battalion for Anti-Aircraft Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does it fall under the artillery of the operation zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't fall within the artillery of the operation zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you personally have absolutely no jurisdiction over this unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document, 4D1629. This is also from the operation zone. The signatory was also your commander, and the payroll for April. We see from this document that on behalf of the HVO, around 5500 personnel were engaged in the operation zone. In the rocket artillery regiment, 350 troops. Is that correct, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the commander of the operation zone, Mr. Lasic, co-issued this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at 4D1534, and I would appreciate your comments. This is an order issued by the commander of the operation zone on the 1st of June, 1993. Tell us, please, whether this was indeed Mico Lasic who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this document. I drafted it myself, actually. Or, rather, it was drafted upon my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This document forbids the use of Maljutka unless it was technically inspected. When it comes to the technical inspection of artillery pieces, were they done on a regularly basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regular inspection of artillery pieces was carried out on a regular basis and the rocket anti-armour pieces also fall under the artillery sector, and they are mentioned in here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, did you also check the ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When it comes to ammunition, as I've already told you, the ammunition is inspected every time a new batch arrives. The ammunition is then tested, and the use of ammunition is always carried out pursuant to strict regulations. All the ammunition is marked by weight, by colours, and all that you can see in the target practice tables, and commanders of detachments and platoons have to bear the information in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If ammunition is stored in a humid area, can that affect the quality of the ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a rule, ammunition is stored in dry areas. However, if there was possibly contact with humidity, such ammunition was most often excluded from use, or what followed was recalculation and preparation of such ammunition for use in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at 4D1675. Are you familiar with this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is my report. I drafted it myself as part of my obligations as chief of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on the information about the available ammunition contained in this report, what would you say? Could the HVO carry out any offensive operations with such equipment and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Here we can see a number of locations where the artillery weapons were deployed. Can you tell us, please, how was the artillery equipment and towards whom at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you can see some positions that tell us that a majority of our positions faced the Army of Republika Srpska and most of the artillery pieces faced the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, when was it that the HVO aimed its artillery pieces towards the positions of the -- of the BiH positions in your operation zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was after the unfortunate events in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And we're talking about Mostar, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at 4D948. This is an order, issued by the Chief of the Main Staff, dated 7 June 1993. Just a few question with regard to this document. To start with, could you please tell us whether you remember the time at the beginning of June 1993, and do you remember that there was indeed a threat facing the HVO in the Mostar region from the direction of Jablanica on the part of the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Under item 2 an order is issued. According to your knowledge, would you say that forces in Bijelo Polje had been regrouped in order to prevent the onslaught of Muslim forces that was expected at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic. It seems to me that these are all really directive questions asking for yes or no, and according to the rule you ought to ask them in a more open way, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that I'm following the procedure that has been used so far and that has also been used by the Prosecutor. If we are -- have been asking the witness about a document, then we would ask him whether what is in the document is correct or not, and the witness has the right to say yes or no. I don't believe that this is a leading question, because the witness can also say that the information contained in the report is incorrect. However, bearing in mind your opinion about the nature of my questions, I'm going to change the nature of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, under item 7, the most rational use of artillery in the area is being ordered. What can you tell us about this term "most rational"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The term "most rational" is the term that was probably most commonly used when it came to the use of artillery during the war for a number of reasons. First of all, we had to identify a military target with as much efficiency as possible and then open fire as rationally as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At that moment, did the HVO have enough ammunition in its disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the largest extent that rationality of use was conditional upon the rational use of ammunition because the HVO did not have enough ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at item 8. Under item 8 you can read that all the defence lines facing Muslims had to be organised in order to prevent attacks. How would you construe this as a soldier? Was this an order for offensive or defensive activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It arises from this item that two things were at stake. First of all, to arrange positions means to prepare for defence; and to prevent attacks means that further attacks were expected, and that meant engineering obstacles, mines and explosives had to be placed in order to prevent attacks and secure the defence line. All this was for the purposes of defence exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please try and explain the rest of this item. What does it mean to arrange positions in depth, in depth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This means that on certain axes losses of territories could be expected, that some of the parts of the defence line, as it was at the time, were probably going to be abandoned and that reserve positions would have to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at P2712. Are you the author of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This document refers to a novelty in the organisation. What was the novelty about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was written at a time when the conflicts with the units of the BiH Army started, at the time when new defence lines were established, and when it was necessary to deploy certain pieces of equipment in such a way as to allow them to cover some new territories within their range.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document, 4D1676. Are you the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is a report which refers to the correction of aim. Could you please explain this term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When it comes to correction in artillery terms, this means that the initial target elements are corrected in order to improve the aim. And this -- the purpose of that was to have a good aim of the target.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The locations that are referred to in here as the areas where the correction firing is taking place, were those settled areas, or what kind of areas were those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a no-man's land, as it were, no settled areas and no units on any of the sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And during that exercise could you damage anything or anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing that could happen was for us to reveal our own positions. We could not damage anything around the target that we were aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Two more documents about the subject. 4D488 is the first one. This is an order issued by Arif Pasalic. I'm interested in item 3, where it says that the sides are committed to carry out special efforts to protect civilian population. And then under (a) it says that military facilities will be moved to a reasonable distance from hospitals, residential buildings and other public facilities. My question to you, Mr. Maric, is this: Did the BiH Army have some of its military facilities in residential neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an example or two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The command of the 4th Corps was in a settled area, the logistics base as well. The command of the artillery unit, the reserve forces, and quite a few other units of the 4th Corps which were deployed in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the BiH Army ever fire mortar shells from the vicinity of the hospital in East Mostar, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the follow document, which is 4D7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question, but I'll ask the question after the break. It has to do with 3(d). So we're going to break for 20 minutes. We shall resume at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Colonel, please go back to the last document we examined, 4D00 -- sorry, 4D1676. No. Sorry. 4D488. Please read out in your own language what is under 3(d).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Intentional or accidental shelling and sniper activity against civilians shall stop."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Pasalic said that shelling or sniper fire directed against civilians, whether they be intentional or accidental, shall stop. So if I read this sentence, I can reach the following conclusion, that the ABiH used snipers against civilians, and General Pasalic demands that this be stopped. What is your view on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This part of General Pasalic's order confirms that there was indeed intentional and accidental shelling and sniper activity against civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we're really trying to get to the bottom of an issue and you being here helps us in this task, any reasonable Judge might think, by way of a hypothesis, that if the ABiH used this, the HVO would do the same. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would have to see a document and then I could comment. As things stand now, in my work as the chief of artillery and when I was artillery commander, I never either ordered or allowed anybody to open fire on civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, we have relatively short time left. There are a lot of documents that I would like to discuss with you. The next one is 4D754. This is an order issued by the town defence sector commander, dated December 1993. Tell us, did you know Mr. Zlatan Mijo Jelic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Under 1 he says that artillery should be used against observed targets exclusively. Could you please explain this rule of shelling observed targets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The rule is to shell only the observed targets, and we always tried to open fire only on such observed targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Why is observation so important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is important because of the efficiency of fire and avoiding collateral damage, and it is also important because of the amount of ammunition, the use of ammunition. This is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Observation and adjustment of fire, are they connected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Adjustment of fire is carried out from an observation post, which means that you cannot adjust fire if you don't observe your target.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Given item 2 in this order where it says that representatives of international forces should not come under threat, let me ask you this: Do you know that any soldier or officer of the HVO intentionally opened fire in the direction of the international forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was there ever any soldier or officer who opened fire in the direction where he knew there were members of the international forces but did not show any concern as to whether he would hit any of them or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document, which is P187 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question, a basic one. It is an essential one because it is at the very heart of the indictment, regarding the shelling in Mostar. Paragraph 1 is very clear. "Artillery is to be used exclusively against the observed targets," it says. I have a question. Who did the observation work? Was it the artillery unit? It could also be other individuals. Let me give you an example. Let us imagine that the intelligence -- military or civilian intelligence service say that on a specific location there is an ABiH unit. The intelligence is fed back to the artillery unit that has all the grids and ranges and can fire. Unfortunately, those who provided the intelligence were wrong, hence damage caused within the civilian population because there were only civilians there and no military. So there was a mistake when it came to gathering intelligence. Now, back to this language here. Who is to observe? Was it the artillery unit as such or it could have been other units passing on the information, and you as an artillery man, you fire based on specific coordinates that you were provided with, and this unfortunately is going to cause damage among the civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Observation and firing were done by those who belong to the very top echelons of the command in an artillery unit, which means that this was within the purview of the officers of the unit opening fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're telling me under oath that when your unit would fire, you had had prior observations from your officers and that the information only came from your own unit. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Observers as rule and in practice are deployed in such positions where they could best observe everything that goes on on the enemy side. They have all the appropriate equipment for observation, and based on that they can establish the exact location of the target and open fire accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Colonel, but this is an essential question. These observers you are speaking about, are they under your own command or under somebody else's command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Persons, or, rather, officers who were in charge of observation and opening fire are primarily responsible to their immediate superior officer or commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer is more accurate but not quite yet. You say that those who observe are answerable to their immediate superior officer or commander, but I am trying to ascertain whether the superior officer in question is directly answerable to you or is he answerable to other individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they're not answerable to me as the chief of artillery. If they are members of a brigade, then they are answerable to the brigade commander. If they're resubordinated to a lower-ranking unit, then they're answerable to that -- the commander of that lower unit who then in turn informs the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to take a theoretical example that may have not occurred in reality but you might be able to give me an answer that might hope clarify the situation. Let us imagine that General Praljak, HVO commander, asked you to take position on a specific location and to fire, if need be, at the enemy if there is potential risk or the danger of response from the enemy. The observers on the ground, are they answerable to you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I was the one who issued the order, then yes, they are answerable to me if I act as their commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I would like to come back to an answer you have given a bit earlier. It's on page 73, lines 23 and following. The question was like this: "Tell us, was there ever any soldier or officer who opened fire in the direction where he knew there were members of the international forces but did not show any concern as to whether he would hit any of them or not?" Your answer is: "No, of course not." Now, the -- the question is very absolute. You are not asked whether you know about any soldier but whether there was ever any soldier who did something like that. And you not only say no, but you say "of course not." Now, I would like to know how do you know this? You ought to be omniscient to know something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from day one of their engagement in the units to the last day -- or, rather, from the first day of my engagement in the unit, I tried, as did all of my officers, all of my subordinate officers, to use the artillery in the best possible way, and such things just could not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Even letting this stand, the question was not limited to your artillerymen. It was generally any soldier or officer, not any under your command. You would have stood -- you would have had to stand next to every soldier whoever fired in this period a shot in Mostar in order to be able to affirm something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to a unit, there are levels of command and levels of responsibility, which means that a soldier in a position cannot be answerable only to me as his supreme commander. He's answerable to his squad commander, and a squad commander is answerable to the platoon commander. The platoon commander is answerable to the battery commander, and it goes all the way up to the brigade command. Any incident that occurs in a firing position is only possible if the commander of that squad did not carry out his duties conscientiously. And they were all educated and trained to carry out their duties honourably and in a conscientious way. Although one of the lowest positions, it is also one of the most honourable positions in any unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I hear and read the answer you give. Please, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, with your permission I would like to provide an explanation. I believe that your questions had more to do with my question than the witness's answer. I would like to draw attention to the fact that my questions are recorded on page 73, line 20. My first question was this: "[In English] Do you know that any soldier intentionally opened fire," [Interpretation] and then I received an answer to the effect that there was no direct intention. I wanted to ask a question about what we lawyers refer to as possible intention, and I believe that I could do a follow-up be -- without repeating my introduction which read, "Do you know that." All my questions try to elicit answers from the direct knowledge of this witness in order to achieve what is known as objective reality, if such a thing exists in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. It's very kind of you to explain to me. I do not think that I have misunderstood, but I think you can go on simply now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document, Mr. Maric, number P1879. I would kindly ask for your comment upon one part of this report which emanated from your operation zone. Under item 4 on your page 3, I'm going to quote the lower part of the text and then I would like to invite your comment. This is a report from the Rama Brigade. "We have forbidden opening artillery fire until the moment an order is received for action, until the moment responsible commanders are appointed for the sectors and areas of responsibility, until the moment observation posts are established, and until the moment wire connection is established with that observation post in order to be able to follow fire and direct fire. There were some requests to open artillery fire today which was disallowed for the above-mentioned reasons." Mr. Maric, could you please tell us whether this shows the rule and procedure that was followed in the HVO artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was drafted in the way it was requested from the units, the way they were instructed to wage war, and this is something that could have been learned, and it could go only from the higher command. The use and engagement of artillery in the HVO was based on that, and it went from the commander down the scale, and political influences were excluded from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Maric. We'll now briefly move on to the next section about HVO as a legal -- the legal and legitimate army in Bosnia and Herzegovina and a component of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I will abbreviate my questions on this topic. We'll skip one document and look at P476. That is decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina from September 1992. I'm not going to ask you about the details of this decision because it is a topic for us lawyers, but I'll ask you this: We see here that the Constitutional Court annulled the decision on the establishment of HZ HB, and in item 5 it annulled the decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It is not stated here that the decision on the establishment of HVO was annulled.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies to counsel. Kim West for the Office of the Prosecution. Mr. President, I've stood up because I understand now Ms. Alaburic says that she's moving to this decision, and I've looked through the original summary, the second summary and then the most recent summary, and it appears that there's nothing even coming close to this topic there, never mind what the gentleman would say about the topic and what testimony he would give. So I may be mistaken and I would ask Ms. Alaburic to correct me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this moment I don't have the summary with me. I can look at it later. But what is quite certain is that we said we will be discussing with this witness HVO as a component of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. One of the parts of this chapter is proving that the decision to establish the HVO was never annulled. Based on that and based on the current legislation of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we are proving the legality and legitimacy of the HVO, and I believe this chapter is certainly indicated in this summary, although it is not itemised. Your Honours, if our learned friends from the Prosecution need additional time to prepare their cross-examination on this subject, if they are not ready to cross-examine any witness of the Defence on the subject of the HVO as component of armed forces, I absolutely don't mind delaying the cross-examination of this witness for a couple of days if that would help the preparation of the Prosecution. And I believe restricting the possibility to examine a witness is completely contrary to the rules of this Tribunal and the rights of the accused to a fair trial. In the course of a witness's testimony all sorts of subjects can crop up, and if we follow the principle of looking for the truth and a fair trial, we must certainly examine the witnesses on all subjects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The issue here is that the parties should be on notice as to what the witness is going to testify about, not just topic matters but exactly what he's going to say. So not only do I not know what he's going to say about this particular topic, I didn't even know that this document was going to be shown. This is a very political document. This is a gentleman who was in charge of the artillery. Why should the Prosecution expect that this gentleman would speak about this constitutional order and then also have to guess what his exact testimony should be. So I'm not asking for any more time to deal with this, but I think that the fundamental rule in order that we can all be properly prepared and in order that the Trial Chamber can discern what the truth of the matter is, is that we all know what the person is going to say and we clearly don't know that in this case, and I think this is a very flagrant abuse of the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, I believe that the Prosecution received the exhibit lists and this document was mentioned in the list. That's the first thing. Secondly, can you first confirm that you received this document that was mentioned in the list?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, what I -- I can't look through it right now but I'll assume the answer to that is correct, that we did. But specifically on this issue of Defence documents, this is not the first time I've seen this from the Petkovic Defence, where the end of the summary will say that the witness will -- excuse me. The witness will be requested to comment on the documents contained in the chart. Therefore, the documents should be treated as part of the summary. Again that's something that the Prosecution objects to. This is talking about a topic, and I don't think that the Defence can adequately oblige their obligation to tell us exactly what the witness is going to testify to by just suggesting that the mere document because it's present on the list gives us fair notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to discuss the matter on the Bench to see whether Ms. Alaburic can ask a question on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just say one thing? I'm not going ask questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not going to be asking any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For me this document was just a basis for asking a very, very simple question, and that question is going to relate to the fact that this witness is a retired officer of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was going to ask him the same question that I asked all the witnesses who were former officers of the army of the federation. And if I saw this document on the list of any party in these proceedings, it would be completely clear to me what the Prosecution would use it to prove or anyone else. And let me just emphasise that with their own witnesses, the Prosecution countless times introduced documents that had nothing whatsoever to do with the interview of the witnesses or their direct examination. Let me just mention the women who came here as witnesses -- as victim witnesses who had nothing to do and no knowledge of very sophisticated military documents they were asked about. We in the Defence had no objection whatsoever. We were only frustrated because we did not have a competent collocutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask your question. The Judges will tell you whether he can answer or not. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us, speaking of your biography, that you retired as an officer of the Army of the Federation of the Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tell me, did your service -- was your service in the HVO recognised as valid service when you were retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, do you have any knowledge that anyone at any time annulled the decision to establish the HVO or questioned in any way the legitimacy of the HVO army in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were all my questions on the subject, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed. These questions have already been put to other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the same thing I said, and I will ask the same question of any former officer of the army of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next subject I wanted to discuss with you, Mr. Maric, is the joint nature and the co-operation between HVO and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let's look at a few documents. 4D1404. Several documents later. This is one notification by Arif Pasalic to the Municipal Staff of HVO Mostar on the replenishment of ammunition, the level of supply with ammunition in the 1st Mostar Brigade of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is September 1992. Who supplied ammunition to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was supplied by the logistics of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next document, 4D615. This is November 1992. Deputy commander of the Mostar Brigade of the ABiH informs the Main Staff of the HVO about contacts with the command of the Municipal Staff relating to security of the left flank and other areas, et cetera. Based on this, tell me, Mr. Maric, did the ABiH and the HVO co-operate in joint actions against their common enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next document, 4D616. This is a document from Arif Pasalic, again November 1992, an order whose item 4 speaks of making contact in Blagaj with Mr. Puljic or Mr. Lasic. Whose commanders were Mr. Puljic or Mr. Lasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Lasic was commander of the military district of Mostar, and Mr. Puljic was Chief of Staff in the same command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you had to evaluate the co-operation between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in area that time, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That co-operation was without any reservation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you co-operate with your opposite numbers in charge of artillery in the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Setting the example for everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What relations do you have with them today?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He saw me off to The Hague with a message to my mobile telephone, wishing me a safe journey.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could just correct the transcript. No. No. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, 4D10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment I have a small technical question to put to you, Witness, which may have escaped a number of people. On item 3 I see that the departure is organised for the 1st Battalion, that is to go to the Luka barracks. And then I see that the 2nd and 3rd Battalions will leave from the Old Bridge. When I saw that, I wondered whether, as far as you know, close to the Old Bridge or on the Old Bridge there were units of the Mostar Brigade, or whether this was just an area where people assembled and from which the soldiers could leave to go elsewhere. Can you shed some light on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this time when this was written, the 17th of November, there was only one bridge in Mostar because the others had been destroyed by the Army of Republika Srpska. That's where crossings were made. That's where troops assembled and where vehicles took them across the river, the troops of these units placed around Mostar. At that time there were no other installations. A bit further was the Ruza installation. A bit further still was the whole of the JNA. Elektrohercegovina and the facility of Razvitak holding personnel of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but next to the bridge there were no military installations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen carefully to my question. If I understand correctly, you are telling me that the military units crossed the Old Bridge because it was the only bridge still standing and that the crossing of the bridge, according to what I have understood here, could also be done on board a vehicle. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. The vehicles were on the east side where soldiers boarded, the east side of Neretva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The vehicles were on the east bank, and the soldiers had to cross over the bridge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a question to you regarding the previous interrogation by Ms. Alaburic where you were asked about the relations to the other party, I suppose it was, and the question was, did you have good relations and you say, "He saw me off to The Hague with a message to my mobile telephone." I have looked this up and down a few times. I do not know, I did not find out who he, this he was. Who was it that sent you an SMS and wished you a good journey to -- a safe journey to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a high-ranking person in the artillery branch of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who had coffee with me on the 7th of May, 1993, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And is there a reason why you don't give his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't ask for his permission, and if you don't mind, Your Honours, I would rather not say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or perhaps we could move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I do not think it is that important. Unless my colleagues think otherwise, we can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, my colleague is raising a problem as far as I'm concerned. I had understood that this was an ABiH army serviceman. I hadn't realised what his status was. And you're telling us that the 7th of May -- the 7th of May is an important date since it is two days before the 9th of May, and you are telling us that you had a coffee with him in Mostar. My colleague asked you why do you not give us his name, and you said, "I don't wish to give his name unless we were to move into private session." My colleague questions the high rank of this officer of the ABiH. I don't know anything about it. I shall turn to my colleagues and ask them whether they wish to move into private session or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber had rather move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: One question regarding your unity. From the position of an artillery weapon of one army, can you estimate who is the enemy of that army at a given moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Until the beginning of the conflict with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in April and May, at whom were the artillery weapons in your operation zone trained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All artillery assets in the operation zone South-east Herzegovina were trained at units of the Army of Republika Srpska, and these assets served the function of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We have another ten minutes left. I think we'll just have enough time to complete one more subject. The brigade of HVO in Konjic and the unit of HVO in Jablanica, were they part of your operation zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1993, I think, they were under the command of the operation zone South-east Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now you should skip two documents in your binder and look at P18 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question for you. Mrs. Alaburic put an important question. I thought she was going to follow it up, but she moved on to something else. And she put the question to you, which, as far as I'm concerned, lies at the heart of the subject here. Towards what was the artillery directed, and you answered her by saying that the artillery pieces were in the direction of the forces of the Republika Srpska, i.e., the Serbs. As I listened to you, I positioned myself in Mostar and East Mostar, and I was wondering whether the HVO artillery was aimed at East Mostar. So this is my question: I want to know whether the HVO artillery was positioned in the direction of East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood your question correctly, it had to be directed across East Mostar, because the lines of the Army of Republika Srpska were behind the lines of Eastern Mostar on the slopes of Mount Velez, at the foot of Mount Velez. So part of the weapons that were close or behind the lines of Western Mostar had logically to be trained at the units of army -- of the Army of Republika Srpska via Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood. The artillery was aimed at the forces of the Republika Srpska, and you are telling us that East Mostar was, of course, along the trajectory of these weapons. So there are angles always when shells are fired, because the shape is such -- the shape is connected to gravity and an angle has to be set. So this is a highly technical question I'm putting to you. The angle which was set, well, would it avoid a shell from falling accidentally or intentionally on East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The margin of errors was studied at several levels. In artillery, there are systemic and deliberate errors. A deliberate error was not possible, not this kind of error. Whether a systemic error could have occurred, yes, but I cannot recall an actual case. I remember at another position a soldier of the HVO, whose name I know, was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you know as we do, because this is a known fact, that there were civilians in East Mostar who were injured or killed following sniper fire or artillery fire. When civilians are injured or killed, as far as the command where you were is concerned, well, were you asked to report on this and explain that on such and such a day did you fire, what did you do, what was the angle and so on? On the part of your command, did you receive any requests to clarify those shots in the case when civilians had been killed or injured, or were you never asked such kind of question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, about everything that was done we had to inform the superior command. I sent reports covering matters that were within my responsibility as chief of artillery. I did not have that sort of information to send to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not quite answering my question. I wanted to know whether at the request of your superiors you had prepared reports on the firing which may have killed or injured civilians. This could have happened accidentally or after having complied with orders, and that was my question and you didn't answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it could not happen upon any order, because I've not seen such orders. Nobody issued such an orders -- such an order for me to know about it. I'm sure that there were no such orders issued at all. As for collateral damage and whether there was any, I suppose that there might have been. However, using the proportionality principle, the HVO artillery always respected and honoured that principle. According to that principle, if the importance of a target is not much larger than any possible collateral damage, then such target was not targeted or shelled at all, and that was the principle that we all respected.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems to me that there has been a misunderstanding between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti asked you whether you received from your superiors an order to draft a report about the artillery activity that might have caused civilian collateral damage in East Mostar, not an order to open artillery fire but an order to draft a report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never received such an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may put just one more question which is a good follow-up on what has been said so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, do you know that anybody from the territory of East Mostar submitted information to the HVO about the number of victims and the status of dead and killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never heard of any such information. I never was privy to such data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now one minute past 7.00 p.m. We shall resume our hearing tomorrow morning at 9.00, so we would like you to be back tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of January, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
